newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: CIS leaders mull security at summit on Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: CIS leaders mull security at summit on Afghanistan.

text.p: Five Commonwealth of Independent States leaders, concerned about border security following the rise to power in Afghanistan of a radical Islamic militia, gathered in Kazakhstan on Friday to consider a joint response.

Kazakhstan President Nursultan Nazarbayev, speaking ahead of the summit, urged other states on Friday not to interfere in the internal affairs of war-battered Afghanistan. But he told reporters he was prepared to submit a peace formula.

The CIS leaders, meeting at the initiative of Russian President Boris Yeltsin, are especially concerned about security along the southern borders of the former Soviet Central Asian states which the Kremlin sees as its strategic underbelly.
"Unfortunately the interests of many great states are focused there (in Afghanistan)," Nazarbayev said. "Now what is important is not to meddle in the internal affairs."
But Nazarbayev said only his country was in a position to offer a proper peace proposal for Afghanistan.

"I think Kazakhstan is well-positioned to do this as Russia and some other states are not correctly perceived here," he said in a clear reference to Moscow's ill-fated intervention in Afghanistan in 1979-1989.

The Taleban militia, a hardline Islamic group, seized the Afghan capital Kabul last week and their advance north towards CIS borders, some of which are guarded with Russian help, has worried Moscow and some other regional states.
The presidents of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and two of Afghanistan's neighbours -- Tajikistan and Uzbekistan -- attended the summit along with Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
Chernomyrdin has assumed some of Yeltsin's functions as the 65-year-old leader prepares for heart surgery later this year.

Russia's State Duma lower chamber of parliament called on Friday for the United Nations to use diplomatic and other levers "to settle the crisis in the Islamic state of Afghanistan and prevent other states from being dragged into this conflict".
A statement approved by 256 votes to nil supported unspecified measures to urge the U.N. "to end military activity in Afghanistan and restore law and order there".

Russia and other members of the CIS, a loose grouping set up as the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, is most concerned about Tajikistan's 1,500-km (900-mile) frontier with Afghanistan, which is patrolled by Russian-led border guards.
The Afghan border has become an effective front line in a prolonged conflict between the pro-Moscow Tajik government in Dushanbe and Islamic guerrillas based in Afghanistan.
"We are following developments closely," General Andrei Nikolayev, head of the Russian border guards, told Russian Public Television on Thursday.
"I think a proposal will be worked out at this meeting that will ensure our common security in the region," he added.
Alexander Lebed, Yeltsin's outspoken national security adviser, has said Russia should give the Afghan government forced out of Kabul all necessary help to counter the Taleban.

But Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov has poured cold water on Lebed's plans. "We are a long way from sympathising with the Taleban movement, that's clear," he said on Thursday. "But I think we should wait."

Some Russian political experts have suggested Moscow should combine reinforcing guards at the border with helping warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum, an ethnic Uzbek who controls northern Afghanistan.
But most top Moscow officials, haunted by the memory of their intervention in Afghanistan, appear extremely cautious about helping any of the parties in the conflict.
